title: Minimal input dimension for superactivation of one-shot zero-error quantum capacity
problem: Two channels that each transmit no quantum information with zero error in a single use can sometimes transmit a qubit perfectly when used together, an effect called superactivation. Shirokov's examples act on four-dimensional inputs, and Shirokov and Shulman showed that superactivation of two channels is impossible if one of them has a qubit input. What is the smallest input dimension in which it can occur?
result: Three. For any finite collection of channels with two-dimensional inputs, the one-shot zero-error quantum capacity is additive, so qubit channels never superactivate. Two explicit operator systems \(S,T\subset M_3\) have no two-dimensional code individually, while \(S\otimes T\) has the two-dimensional code spanned by \(\ket{00}\) and \((\ket{11}+\ket{22})/\sqrt2\). Channels with these noncommutative graphs therefore superactivate with three-dimensional inputs.
significance: The result pins down the threshold dimension for the simplest form of superactivation, one of the most striking non-additivity effects in quantum Shannon theory, and replaces a four-dimensional example with a three-dimensional one that can be checked by hand. The qubit additivity theorem extends the earlier two-channel impossibility to any number of channels.
limitations: The statement concerns one-shot zero-error capacity, the dimension of a perfect code in a single joint use; the asymptotic zero-error capacity of these channels is not computed. The channels are given only through their noncommutative graphs, realized by a general existence theorem, not as explicit physical channels. The author states that the pair \(S,T\) was obtained with the assistance of GPT-6 Astra, and that all statements were then checked in exact algebraic form.
summary_basis: Description based on the full arXiv HTML of v1, read 2026-11-27: the whole paper, including Lemmas 1–4, Theorem 1, Proposition 1, the code construction of Sec. 4.2 and the AI statement. Editorial checks: for every pair of generators A of S and B of T, the compression P(A ⊗ B)P equals A_00 B_00 P exactly (numerically, to machine precision); and a random search over 20,000 two-dimensional subspaces of C^3 found a smallest Knill–Laflamme defect of 0.29 for S, consistent with Proposition 1's proof that S has no two-dimensional code.

description: A channel \(\Phi(\rho)=\sum_kV_k\rho V_k^\dagger\) determines its noncommutative graph \(S(\Phi)=\mathrm{span}\{V_k^\dagger V_l\}\), an operator system containing the identity and closed under adjoints. A subspace with projector \(P\) is a perfect quantum code exactly when \(PXP\) is a multiple of \(P\) for every \(X\in S(\Phi)\), the Knill–Laflamme condition. The one-shot zero-error quantum capacity is \(\log_2\) of the largest such code. Graphs of product channels are tensor products, \(S(\Phi_1\otimes\Phi_2)=S(\Phi_1)\otimes S(\Phi_2)\).

For qubit inputs the paper shows that every operator system in \(M_2\) is either the scalars, where the whole qubit is a code, or contains a copy of the diagonal algebra \(D_2\) after a change of basis. A tensor product of \(k\) scalar factors and \(n-k\) diagonal factors has largest code dimension exactly \(2^k\), so codes for products of qubit channels come only from factors that are already perfect, and the capacity adds.

In dimension three the construction uses \(S=\mathrm{span}\{I,E_{01},E_{10},H_+\}\) and \(T=\mathrm{span}\{I,E_{02},E_{20},H_-\}\), with \(H_\pm\) acting on the last two basis vectors as \(\begin{pmatrix}1&\pm1\\\pm1&-1\end{pmatrix}\). The rank-one elements \(E_{01}\) and \(E_{02}\) force any two-dimensional code into a coordinate plane, where \(H_\pm\) compresses to a non-scalar matrix, so neither system has a code. In the product, the off-diagonal generators were chosen so that the cross terms between \(\ket{00}\) and \((\ket{11}+\ket{22})/\sqrt2\) vanish, and the trace conditions on the blocks of \(H_\pm\) make the diagonal entries equal.

methods.technique: Every non-scalar qubit graph contains a diagonal algebra
methods.explanation: To prove additivity for qubits, one needs a uniform upper bound on codes for any product. Shrinking each non-scalar factor to a diagonal subsystem only enlarges the set of codes, and diagonal algebras have codes that are easy to count.
math: Monotonicity: if \(T\subseteq S\) then every code for \(S\) is a code for \(T\), so \(\alpha_q(S)\le\alpha_q(T)\). A non-scalar \(S\subset M_2\) contains a non-scalar Hermitian \(H\) with distinct eigenvalues, and \(\mathrm{span}\{I,H\}\) is unitarily equivalent to \(D_2\). Hence a product of \(k\) scalar and \(n-k\) non-scalar factors satisfies \[\alpha_q\Bigl(\textstyle\bigotimes_iS_i\Bigr)\le\alpha_q\bigl(\mathbb CI_{2^k}\otimes D_{2^{n-k}}\bigr).\]

For \(\mathbb CI_m\otimes D_r\), write code vectors as \(\ket{\psi_\ell}=\sum_j\ket{u_{\ell j}}\otimes\ket j\). The Knill–Laflamme conditions for all diagonal \(D_r\) elements give \(\langle u_{\ell j}|u_{sj}\rangle=0\) for \(\ell\ne s\) and equal norms \(\|u_{\ell j}\|\) for all \(\ell\). More than \(m\) code vectors would require more than \(m\) orthogonal vectors of equal norm in \(\mathbb C^m\), forcing them all to zero. So \(\alpha_q=m=2^k\), matched by the code \((\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes k}\otimes\ket\eta\), and \(\overline Q_0\) is exactly the number of scalar factors.
methods.transfer: Bounding codes for a product by those of a smaller, structured subsystem turns an optimization over subspaces into a counting argument. The same reduction can test additivity of zero-error quantities in other small dimensions.

methods.technique: Designing two graphs whose product admits an entangled code
methods.explanation: Superactivation needs a code for \(S\otimes T\) that is not a product of codes. The generators of \(S\) and \(T\) are chosen so that, on one entangled vector and one product vector, all off-diagonal Knill–Laflamme terms vanish by support and all diagonal terms agree by trace identities.
math: Let \(\ket u=\ket{00}\) and \(\ket v=(\ket{11}+\ket{22})/\sqrt2\). For \(A\in S\), \(B\in T\), \[\langle u|A\otimes B|v\rangle=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\bigl(A_{01}B_{01}+A_{02}B_{02}\bigr)=0,\] since \(S\) has no \(E_{02}\) component and \(T\) no \(E_{01}\) component; the same holds for \(\langle v|A\otimes B|u\rangle\).

On the lower block, \(A'=aI_2+xD_+\) and \(B'=bI_2+yD_-\) with \(a=A_{00}\), \(b=B_{00}\), and \[\langle v|A\otimes B|v\rangle=\tfrac12\mathrm{Tr}\bigl(A'^{T}B'\bigr)=ab+\tfrac{ay}2\mathrm{Tr}D_-+\tfrac{bx}2\mathrm{Tr}D_++\tfrac{xy}2\mathrm{Tr}(D_+^TD_-)=ab,\] because \(\mathrm{Tr}D_\pm=0\) and \(\mathrm{Tr}(D_+^TD_-)=1-1-1+1=0\). This equals \(\langle u|A\otimes B|u\rangle=ab\), so \(P(S\otimes T)P=\mathbb CP\). Editorial check: the identity \(P(A\otimes B)P=A_{00}B_{00}P\) holds numerically for all 16 generator pairs.
methods.transfer: Choosing generators whose supports avoid each other and whose blocks are trace-orthogonal is a direct recipe for entangled zero-error codes. A computer search over such sparse operator systems, then exact verification, is how this example was found.
